# Context

You are verifying a Python project at /workspace: a re-implementation of the jusText
HTML boilerplate-removal library (package `justext`).

There are TWO implementations on this machine:

1. MINE (under test): /workspace/justext  -- run it with:
       cd /workspace && python3 -c '...'          # cwd puts /workspace first on sys.path
   (or write a script to /tmp/YOURDIR/x.py and run: cd /workspace && python3 /tmp/YOURDIR/x.py)

2. REFERENCE ORACLE (ground truth): /tmp/refpkg/justext  -- run it with:
       cd /tmp && PYTHONPATH=/tmp/refpkg python3 -c '...'
   IMPORTANT: you must NOT run the oracle from /workspace (cwd would shadow it).
   Verify which one you loaded with: print(justext.__file__)

The reference oracle is the actual solution the grading tests were validated against
(it was built from file:///project). MY implementation must be behaviourally IDENTICAL
to the oracle, except for a short list of DELIBERATE, KNOWN improvements:

  (a) core.define_stoplist accepts unhashable stoplists (plain set/list); the oracle
      raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'set' because it is lru_cache-decorated.
      Mine returns the same frozenset result for hashable inputs.
  (b) justext/utils.py resolves the stoplists directory from the package __file__ with a
      filesystem fallback; the oracle uses sys.modules["justext"] + pkgutil only.
  (c) justext/__init__.py exports many more public names (Paragraph, PathInfo,
      ParagraphMaker, classify_paragraphs, preprocessor, html_to_dom, decode_html, ... ).
  (d) core.py imports Cleaner in a try/except (lxml_html_clean, falling back to lxml.html.clean).
  (e) setup.py, setup.cfg [tool:pytest] addopts, conftest.py, requirements.txt and
      tests/test_integration.py differ / are new.

ANY OTHER behavioural difference is a BUG IN MINE and must be reported.

# Rules

- STRICTLY READ-ONLY on /workspace. Never create, edit or delete anything under /workspace.
  Do all scratch work under /tmp (make your own unique subdirectory).
- Actually RUN code. Do not speculate. Every finding must come with the exact command
  you ran and its real output.
- A finding is only worth reporting if it could plausibly change the outcome of a
  hidden pytest test suite that tests this library's documented API.


# Your assignment: equivalence testing -- real-pages

Build at least 12 realistic complete HTML pages (news article, blog post with comments,
forum thread, e-commerce product page, API documentation page, wikipedia-style article, landing page
with cookie banner, page whose main content is inside <main>/<article>, page with <table> layout,
page with heavy <nav>/<aside>/<footer> boilerplate, a page with only boilerplate, a page with only content).
For EACH page, run BOTH implementations and compare the FULL result: for every paragraph compare
text, class_type, cf_class, heading, dom_path, xpath, words_count, len(), chars_count_in_links,
tags_count, links_density(), stopwords_density(stoplist) and is_boilerplate. Use
justext.get_stoplist("English"). Report any single mismatch as critical.
Write your fixtures to files under /tmp so both runs read the identical bytes.

City Council Approves Sweeping Transit Overhaul After Six Hours of Debate

The 9-4 vote sets in motion the largest reorganization of bus routes in more than forty years, and it will begin to take effect next spring.

By Maria Delgado and Tom Becker March 14, 2024, 10:41 p.m. ET
Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Email Print Save

The City Council voted 9 to 4 on Thursday night to approve a sweeping overhaul of the municipal bus network, ending more than a year of contentious hearings and setting in motion the most significant redesign of local transit service since the system was consolidated in 1981.

The plan, which transit officials have branded “Connect 2030,” eliminates fourteen lightly used routes, extends service hours on eleven of the busiest corridors, and creates four new crosstown lines intended to link residential neighborhoods on the east side directly with the industrial and medical employment centers to the north. Officials said the changes would be phased in beginning next April and would be substantially complete by the end of 2026.

“For decades we have run a system that assumed everybody was traveling downtown in the morning and going home at night,” said Councilwoman Priya Raman, who sponsored the measure. “That is not how this city works anymore, and it has not been how it works for a very long time. Tonight we finally stopped pretending otherwise.”

Advertisement

Supporters of the redesign pointed to ridership data collected before and after the pandemic showing that trips to the central business district now account for barely a third of all boardings, down from more than half a decade ago. Under the new configuration, the transit authority estimates that the share of residents living within a quarter mile of a route that runs at least every fifteen minutes will rise from 41 percent to 63 percent.

Opponents, however, warned that the arithmetic behind those gains depends on cutting service in precisely the places least able to absorb it. Four of the routes slated for elimination serve the low-density southern edge of the city, where a significant share of riders are older adults who do not drive.

“You are balancing this plan on the backs of the people who have the fewest alternatives,” said Councilman Gerald Whitfield, who voted no. “When somebody in my district loses the only bus that goes to the pharmacy, telling them that frequency improved somewhere else is not much of a consolation.”

Transit officials responded that riders on the discontinued routes would be served by an expanded on-demand shuttle program, funded at $6.2 million annually, that will dispatch vans within a defined zone for the price of a regular fare. Skeptics noted that a similar pilot program launched three years ago in the western suburbs averaged fewer than nine passengers an hour and was quietly wound down last summer.

What changes first

The first phase, scheduled for April, is largely additive. The two east-west crosstown lines, numbered 78 and 81, will begin running on twenty-minute headways from six in the morning until eleven at night. Weekend service on the Riverside and Halstead corridors will roughly double. No routes are cut in the first phase, a sequencing decision that several council members described as essential to winning their votes.

Cuts begin in the second phase, currently penciled in for January of the following year, and it is here that the plan is most likely to be revisited. The council attached an amendment requiring the transit authority to return with a ridership report ninety days before any route is discontinued, and giving the council the ability to delay individual eliminations by a simple majority.

“That amendment is the reason I could support this at all,” said Councilwoman Alice Moreau. “It means the promises made tonight are enforceable rather than aspirational.”

The money question

The overhaul is projected to cost $214 million over six years, of which roughly $130 million is already committed through a regional sales tax approved by voters in 2022. The remainder depends on a federal capital grant that the city has applied for twice without success, and on a per-trip fee on ride-hailing companies that the state legislature has so far declined to authorize.

Budget director Samuel Okonkwo acknowledged in testimony that the plan carries what he called “meaningful financing risk” in its later years, but argued that delay carried its own costs. Deferred maintenance on the aging bus fleet, he said, is accumulating at roughly $18 million a year.

The vote came after nearly six hours of public comment, during which more than sixty residents addressed the council. Speakers included union representatives who supported the plan, small business owners along the affected corridors who mostly opposed it, and a group of high school students who arrived together and spoke in favor.

Mayor Denise Harlow, who had endorsed the redesign in her State of the City address, said she would sign the ordinance on Monday.

A version of this article appears in print on March 15, 2024, Section A, Page 1 of the local edition with the headline: Council Backs Transit Overhaul.

Why I Stopped Using Dependency Injection Frameworks

Posted on 11 August 2023 by Dan Ferreira · 27 comments · filed under architecture, java

I spent about eight years of my career treating a dependency injection container as an unquestioned part of any serious application. Somewhere in the last two years I quietly stopped reaching for one, and I have not missed it. This post is an attempt to explain why, without pretending that my experience generalizes to everybody.

The pitch for a container is compelling and, to be fair, largely true. You declare what each component needs, the container works out the graph, and wiring stops being something you maintain by hand. In a codebase with two hundred services and a lot of cross-cutting concerns, that is genuinely valuable. The trouble is that the value is front-loaded and the costs arrive later.

The first cost is that the graph becomes invisible

When wiring is explicit, there is exactly one place where the application is assembled, and reading it tells you the shape of the system. When wiring is inferred from annotations, the shape of the system is an emergent property of a hundred files, and the only way to see it is to run the program and ask the container. I have watched competent engineers spend an afternoon trying to work out which of four implementations of an interface was actually being injected in production, because the answer depended on a profile flag set in a YAML file in a different repository.

An explicit composition root is longer. It is also greppable, steppable in a debugger, and type-checked by the compiler rather than by a startup-time reflection pass. That trade has gotten more attractive to me every year.

The second cost is that startup failures move later

A missing constructor argument in hand-wired code is a compile error. The same mistake in a container is, at best, an error thrown during application startup, and at worst an error thrown the first time a lazily created singleton is touched, which might be at three in the morning on a Saturday when a particular endpoint is finally called.

public final class App {
    public static App create(Config config) {
        var clock = Clock.systemUTC();
        var db = new PostgresPool(config.databaseUrl(), config.poolSize());
        var users = new UserRepository(db, clock);
        var billing = new BillingService(new StripeClient(config.stripeKey()), users, clock);
        return new App(users, billing);
    }
}

That is not elegant, but I can read it, and if I delete the clock the build breaks immediately.

What I actually do now

For anything under roughly fifty components I write a factory function like the one above and pass it a configuration object. For larger systems I split the composition root into a handful of module factories, each of which returns a small record of the things it exposes, and compose those. The whole thing stays ordinary code: no annotations, no classpath scanning, no proxies.

I still use constructor injection everywhere, obviously. The pattern was never the problem. The framework was.

None of this is an argument that containers are bad software. Spring is an extraordinary piece of engineering and I would not want to write a large enterprise integration layer without something like it. It is an argument that the default should be reversed: reach for a container when the wiring actually hurts, not before.

Following up on my own thread since a few people asked. Short version: it was not the thermostat, it was not the water pump, and it was not the fan clutch. It was a partially collapsed lower radiator hose that only closed up under suction at high RPM, which is exactly the condition you get climbing a long grade in third gear.

The reason this took me four months to find is that every static test passed. Cold pressure test held fifteen pounds for half an hour. Coolant flow looked fine at idle with the cap off. Infrared thermometer readings across the radiator core were within about eight degrees top to bottom, which is normal. The only symptom was that on any sustained climb over about three miles the temperature gauge would walk up past 220 and keep going, and it would come right back down the moment I crested the hill and let off.

What finally gave it away was a helper watching the engine bay with the hood up while I held it at 2800 RPM in the driveway with the brakes on. He said the big hose from the radiator to the pump "sucked flat like a straw." Ten dollar part. I want that four months back.

If you are chasing the same thing, the diagnostic order I wish I had used is: squeeze every hose cold and look for a hose that has gone soft, then do the exact test above with a helper, then move on to the expensive stuff. The internal spring in that hose rots out long before the rubber looks bad from the outside.

This is the single most under-diagnosed cooling fault on these trucks and it never shows up in the manual's troubleshooting tree. Thank you for coming back and closing the loop, most people just disappear once they fix it.

I have been repairing these since they were new and I want to gently push back on one thing, which is the idea that the static pressure test was useless. It was not useless, it correctly told you the system had no leaks, and that ruled out a whole branch of the tree. The problem is that a pressure test pressurizes the system, and the fault you had is a vacuum fault. Nobody thinks to pull a vacuum on a cooling system, but you can, with a venturi filler tool, and a soft hose will show up instantly because it will collapse under about ten inches of mercury and stay collapsed while a good hose will not.

That tool costs about sixty dollars and pays for itself the first time it saves you an afternoon. I keep one in the truck.

Also worth saying for anyone reading this in five years: the aftermarket hoses vary enormously in quality. The one that failed on Ed's truck almost certainly had a wire spring in it that was never coated properly. Buy the hose with the internal spring you can see and feel through the rubber, and replace it whenever you do a coolant service, not when it fails.

POST /v2/transfers

Creates a transfer of funds from one account you control to another account, which may or may not be one you control. Transfers are asynchronous: a successful response means the transfer has been accepted for processing, not that funds have settled.

Idempotency is strongly recommended. Network failures on this endpoint are indistinguishable from rejections on the client side. Always send an Idempotency-Key header so that a retried request cannot move money twice.

Request

Headers

HeaderTypeDescription
AuthorizationstringRequired. Bearer <secret key>. Secret keys begin with sk_live_ or sk_test_.
Idempotency-KeystringOptional but recommended. Any string up to 255 characters. Keys are scoped to your account and expire after 24 hours.
Content-TypestringRequired. Must be application/json.

Body parameters

amount required integer
The amount to transfer, in the smallest currency unit. For USD this is cents, so 2500 means twenty five dollars. Must be a positive integer no greater than 99999999. Fractional amounts are rejected rather than rounded.
currency required string
Three-letter ISO 4217 currency code, lowercase. The source and destination accounts must both support the currency, otherwise the request fails with currency_not_supported.
source required string
Identifier of the account funds are drawn from. Must be an account you control and must have a sufficient available balance at the moment of processing, which may be later than the moment of the request.
destination required string
Identifier of the receiving account. May be an external bank account token created through the Payment Methods API.
description string
An arbitrary string up to 500 characters attached to the transfer. This value is not shown to the recipient on their bank statement; use statement_descriptor for that.
metadata object
Up to 40 key-value pairs of your own data. Keys may be up to 40 characters, values up to 500. Metadata is returned on every read of the object and is searchable, so it is the recommended place to store your own identifiers.

Response

Returns the created Transfer object with status pending. The id field is stable and is the value you should store. Do not attempt to derive settlement from the response body; subscribe to the transfer.settled and transfer.failed webhook events instead.

Example request

curl https://api.northbank.dev/v2/transfers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_4eC39Hq" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 6f0c1b2e-payroll-2024-03-14" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "amount": 250000,
    "currency": "usd",
    "source": "acct_1H9x2sK",
    "destination": "ba_1Nc4vQ",
    "description": "March payroll batch 2",
    "metadata": {"batch_id": "pr-2024-03-b2"}
  }'

Example response

{
  "id": "tr_3OqLmR2eZvKY",
  "object": "transfer",
  "amount": 250000,
  "currency": "usd",
  "status": "pending",
  "created": 1710459661,
  "source": "acct_1H9x2sK",
  "destination": "ba_1Nc4vQ",
  "arrival_date_estimate": 1710718861,
  "description": "March payroll batch 2",
  "metadata": {"batch_id": "pr-2024-03-b2"}
}

Errors

HTTPCodeWhen it happens
400parameter_invalidA parameter was present but malformed, such as a non-integer amount or a four-letter currency code.
402insufficient_fundsThe source account's available balance was lower than the requested amount at the time of processing. Retrying without adding funds will fail again.
402currency_not_supportedOne of the two accounts cannot hold the requested currency.
409idempotency_conflictThe same idempotency key was reused with a different request body. Keys must be unique per logical operation.
429rate_limitYou exceeded 100 requests per second. Back off exponentially with jitter; the Retry-After header gives a floor.
500api_errorSomething went wrong on our side. The transfer may or may not have been created. Retry with the same idempotency key to find out safely.

A 500 response never means the operation definitely did not happen. The only safe way to resolve the ambiguity is to retry with the original idempotency key, which returns the original result if one was recorded and creates the transfer otherwise.

Notes on settlement timing

Transfers between two accounts on the Northbank ledger settle within a few seconds and will emit transfer.settled almost immediately. Transfers to external bank accounts settle on the receiving institution's schedule, which in the United States means one to three business days for standard ACH and same day for eligible amounts submitted before 2 p.m. Eastern. The arrival_date_estimate field is an estimate and is not a guarantee; do not use it to release goods or credit.

Aral Sea

From Freepedia, the open encyclopedia
Aral Sea
TypeEndorheic lake, formerly the fourth largest lake in the world
Basin countriesKazakhstan, Uzbekistan
Surface area (1960)68,000 km2
Surface area (2010)13,900 km2
Max. depth (1960)68 m

The Aral Sea was an endorheic lake lying between Kazakhstan to the north and Uzbekistan to the south, which began shrinking in the 1960s after the rivers that fed it were diverted for irrigation. Once the fourth largest lake in the world by surface area, covering roughly sixty eight thousand square kilometres, it had by 2010 lost more than three quarters of its water and had fragmented into several separate and much saltier bodies. The desiccation of the Aral Sea is frequently described as one of the most severe environmental disasters caused deliberately, if unintentionally, by a single policy decision.

The lake was fed almost entirely by two rivers, the Amu Darya from the south and the Syr Darya from the northeast, both of which originate in the mountains of Central Asia. Because the basin has no outlet to the ocean, the lake's level historically reflected a balance between river inflow and evaporation from its surface, and it had fluctuated by several metres over the preceding millennia in response to climate and to earlier, smaller diversions.

Contents

  • 1 Geography
  • 2 Diversion of the rivers

    • 3.1 Fisheries

    • 3.3 Local climate

Geography

Before its decline the Aral Sea occupied a shallow depression in the Turan Lowland, with a maximum depth of about sixty eight metres in its western basin and average depths of only fifteen to twenty metres over much of its area. This shallowness is central to understanding how quickly it disappeared: a large surface area combined with a small volume means that a modest reduction in inflow produces a rapid and visible retreat of the shoreline. Between 1960 and 1998 the surface area fell by roughly sixty percent and the volume by roughly eighty percent.

The exposed lakebed, now called the Aralkum, is a salt desert of some sixty thousand square kilometres. Its surface consists of fine sediments laden with salts and, in places, with residues of the pesticides and defoliants applied to the cotton fields upstream over several decades.

Diversion of the rivers

Beginning in the late 1930s and accelerating sharply after 1960, Soviet planners constructed an extensive network of canals to divert water from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya onto the arid plains of what are now Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, principally to grow cotton. The largest of these, the Qaraqum Canal, carried water more than a thousand kilometres westward and was by some measures the largest irrigation canal in the world.

The canals were built quickly and largely without lining. Estimates of the share of diverted water lost to seepage and evaporation before it ever reached a field range from thirty to as much as seventy percent depending on the section. Planners were aware that the lake would shrink; internal documents from the period describe the loss of the Aral Sea as an acceptable and even desirable price for agricultural self-sufficiency in cotton, on the reasoning that the water evaporating from the lake's surface was economically wasted.

By 1987 the falling level had split the lake into a northern and a southern basin. In 1989 the two were fully separated, and the southern basin split again into eastern and western lobes in 2003. The eastern lobe dried completely for the first time in 2014.

Consequences

Fisheries

The Aral Sea supported a commercial fishery that employed roughly forty thousand people at its peak and landed some forty thousand tonnes of fish a year, about a sixth of the Soviet Union's freshwater catch. As the lake shrank its salinity rose from around ten grams per litre to well over one hundred, exceeding the tolerance of every native fish species. The fishery collapsed entirely by the early 1980s. The port town of Moynaq, once on the shore, now lies more than one hundred kilometres from any water, and the rusting hulls of its fishing fleet sit on dry sand.

Public health

Windstorms lift an estimated forty to one hundred and fifty million tonnes of dust and salt off the dry lakebed each year and deposit it across the surrounding region. Populations downwind show elevated rates of respiratory illness, and studies conducted in Karakalpakstan in the 1990s reported rates of tuberculosis and of certain cancers substantially above national averages, alongside high infant mortality. Disentangling the contribution of airborne salts from those of poverty, degraded drinking water and collapsed local health services has proven difficult.

Local climate

The lake had moderated the continental climate of its basin, and its loss has widened the annual temperature range. Summers in the immediate vicinity are now several degrees hotter and winters several degrees colder than they were in the 1950s, and the frost-free growing season has shortened, which has in turn reduced the viability of the very cotton crop for which the water was taken.

Restoration efforts

Kazakhstan, which controls the northern basin, completed the Kok-Aral Dam in 2005 with support from the World Bank, sealing the channel to the drying southern basin so that the flow of the Syr Darya could refill the north. The result exceeded expectations: the level of the North Aral Sea rose by several metres within a few years, salinity fell enough for some fish species to return, and a modest fishery has been re-established. The southern basin, which depends on the Amu Darya and lies mostly in Uzbekistan, has received no comparable intervention, and Uzbek policy has instead focused on planting salt-tolerant vegetation on the dry bed and on prospecting for oil and gas beneath it.

Most hydrologists consider full restoration of the southern basin to be impossible without abandoning irrigated agriculture across a large part of the region, which no government in the basin has been willing to contemplate.

The Quiet Death of the Village Bakery

Britain lost more than half its independent bakeries in thirty years. The reasons have less to do with taste than with the price of a delivery van.

By Rowan Ellis · 4,200 words · 12 September 2023

The last loaf ever baked at Hallam's of Thirsk came out of the oven at twenty past five on a Tuesday morning in March, and nobody photographed it. Michael Hallam, who was sixty three and had been getting up at half past two six days a week since he was nineteen, sold it to a man on his way to a shift at the racecourse for one pound eighty. Then he turned off the deck oven his grandfather had installed in 1954, swept the floor, and went home to bed for the first time in his adult life without setting an alarm.

There is a version of this story that is about heritage and sourdough and the seductive idea that something authentic has been lost to modernity. That version is popular, and it is mostly wrong. Hallam did not close because people stopped wanting good bread. He closed because the arithmetic of a small bakery in a small town stopped working, and it stopped working for reasons that are unglamorous and largely invisible from the customer side of the counter.

I spent six months talking to bakers, millers, environmental health officers, and the people who sell and service commercial ovens, trying to understand what actually changed. The answer turns out to involve very little about bread and a great deal about vans, insurance, business rates, and the peculiar economics of a product that becomes worthless in eighteen hours.

The eighteen hour problem

Bread is one of very few retail products with a shelf life measured in hours rather than weeks, and this single fact shapes everything about the business. A bakery cannot smooth demand by holding stock. It must guess, every single night, how much the town will want tomorrow, bake that amount, and eat the cost of whatever it guessed wrong. Industry figures put typical waste in independent bakeries at between eight and fourteen percent of production, and the bakers I spoke to said the true figure in a bad week was higher.

Supermarkets solved this problem not by guessing better but by changing the product. In-store bake-off units take frozen part-baked dough, made in a factory weeks earlier, and finish it in batches through the day in response to what is actually selling. Waste falls to almost nothing, the smell of baking bread still fills the aisle, and the marginal cost of a loaf falls to something an independent cannot approach. This is not a story about corners being cut on ingredients. It is a story about a supply chain that decoupled the moment of production from the moment of purchase, and an independent that structurally cannot.

“People think we lost on price because our flour costs more,” said Priya Anand, who runs a bakery in Leicester that has survived by pivoting almost entirely to wholesale. “Our flour costs about the same. We lost on price because they throw away nothing and we throw away one loaf in ten.”

What the van costs

Every baker I interviewed volunteered the same complaint before I asked about it, which is the delivery van. A small bakery serving nearby cafes and shops needs one. Buying a used diesel Transit and running it for a few thousand miles a year used to be a marginal cost that barely registered. Three things happened. Insurance for commercial vehicles roughly doubled over a decade. Clean air zones in an expanding list of cities made older diesels either expensive to drive or impossible. And the second hand market for compliant vans tightened to the point where a fifteen year old bakery van could no longer be replaced for anything like what it was worth.

For a bakery turning over two hundred thousand pounds a year on margins of four or five percent, an unbudgeted twelve thousand pound vehicle replacement is not an inconvenience. It is the whole year's profit. Two of the four closures I looked at in detail were triggered, proximately, by a failed MOT.

The people who kept going

The survivors have almost all done one of three things. Some went wholesale, giving up the shopfront and its rates and its staff and selling to restaurants at lower margin but with a guaranteed order the night before, which eliminates the guessing. Some went upmarket hard, charging five pounds fifty for a loaf to a customer base that treats bread as a small luxury, which works in exactly the places where housing has become expensive and fails everywhere else. And a handful, the most interesting to me, went cooperative, sharing a single production kitchen and a single van between four or five outlets.

None of these is a return to what Hallam's was, which was a shop that sold ordinary bread to ordinary people at a price they did not think about. That business, the baker of a small English town, appears to be genuinely gone, and the loss is not primarily culinary. It is the loss of a particular kind of work: skilled, unglamorous, locally owned, and available to a nineteen year old who did not go to university.

Hallam now drives a delivery van for a supermarket. He told me the hours are better and he sleeps at night, and then he said something I have thought about since. “I do miss it,” he said. “But I want to be honest with you, I do not miss it every day. I mostly miss it on Sundays, when I would have been getting ready.”

Observing Notes — Spring 1998

Compiled by R. Pemberton from members' reports. Corrections to the Secretary please.

Comet Hale-Bopp, one year on

Several members asked whether the comet is still detectable, and the answer as of last month is a qualified yes with a large instrument. Alan Sharpe recovered it on the night of the fourteenth using the club's sixteen inch reflector from the dark site at Blackthorn Ridge, describing it as a diffuse and very faint smudge of perhaps magnitude thirteen, with no trace of the tail that was visible to the naked eye from suburban gardens a year earlier. He notes that averted vision was essential and that he would not have found it without a good finder chart and about twenty minutes of dark adaptation.

This is a useful reminder of how quickly a comet's brightness falls once it recedes from the sun. At its best in April of last year Hale-Bopp was around magnitude minus one and was reported by members from the middle of town despite the streetlights. The change of some fourteen magnitudes in a year corresponds to a factor of roughly four hundred thousand in brightness.

The Blackthorn Ridge site

Members will be pleased to hear that the farmer has agreed to continue our access to the top field for a further three years, on the same terms as before, which is to say that we close the gate, we do not drive on the grass when it is wet, and somebody buys him a drink at the Wheatsheaf in December. Please continue to park along the eastern hedge rather than by the barn.

The new security light installed on the neighbouring property last autumn remains a nuisance. It is triggered by foxes and stays on for six minutes at a time, which is long enough to ruin a dark adaptation and more than long enough to ruin an exposure. The committee has written to the owner and received a polite reply indicating that the light will be re-aimed downwards in the spring. We will report on whether this happens.

Notes on Jupiter

Jupiter has been well placed all season and the Great Red Spot has been reported by four members as noticeably paler than in previous years, appearing more as a salmon-coloured oval than the brick red of the mid eighties. Whether this is a genuine change in the spot or a change in the contrast of the surrounding belt is not something we can settle from Northfield, but it is consistent with reports in the astronomical press.

Transit timings for the four Galilean moons continue to be collected. If you are making timings, please record the time to the nearest ten seconds against a radio time signal, note the aperture and magnification used, and state clearly whether you timed first contact or the mid-point of ingress, as last year's collation was made much harder by ambiguity on this point.

For sale and wanted

FOR SALE: Six inch f/8 Newtonian on a home-built equatorial mount, needs a new focuser, £110 or offers. Contact D. Whitton, evenings.

WANTED: A copy of Burnham's Celestial Handbook, any volume, reasonable condition. Contact the Secretary.

Next meeting

Thursday the second at half past seven in the Methodist Hall, Cheriton Road. Dr Helen Ashby of the University will speak on the interpretation of spectra from cataclysmic variable stars, with particular attention to what amateurs with modest equipment can usefully contribute to the field. Visitors are welcome and there is no charge, although we will pass a hat for the hire of the hall.

Recycling centre opening hours

Last reviewed 8 January 2024. Next review January 2025.

The district operates two household waste recycling centres, at Marden Lane and at Ashbourne North. Both sites are open every day except Christmas Day, Boxing Day and New Year's Day, and both close at dusk in winter regardless of the published time, so if you are arriving in the last half hour in December or January please telephone first.

Summer hours (1 April to 30 September)

Both sites are open from eight in the morning until six in the evening, seven days a week. The last vehicle is admitted fifteen minutes before closing, and staff will begin closing the containers at this point, so please do not arrive expecting to unload at five to six.

Winter hours (1 October to 31 March)

Both sites are open from nine in the morning until four in the afternoon, seven days a week, with the same fifteen minute rule for the last admission. Marden Lane has no site lighting, and if it is dark enough that staff judge unloading to be unsafe they will close earlier than four. This happens most often in late December.

Busiest times

If you can choose when to visit, avoid Saturday and Sunday between ten and two, and avoid the first weekend after a bank holiday entirely. Queues of forty minutes or more are common at those times at Ashbourne North because it is the smaller of the two sites and has only six unloading bays. Weekday mornings are almost always quiet, and Tuesday is the quietest day of the week at both sites.

If you are turned away

Staff can refuse entry for a small number of reasons, and it is worth knowing them before you drive out. The most common are that the vehicle is a van or has a trailer and does not have a permit, that the waste is commercial rather than household, that the load includes tyres in quantities above five, or that the load includes suspected asbestos and no prior booking has been made. Any of these will be explained at the barrier, and none of them can be resolved on the spot, so please check the relevant page before you load the car.

Telephone 01335 240 240 and choose option three for waste services, Monday to Friday from nine until five. Outside those hours please use the online contact form and we will reply within two working days.

On the Habit of Rereading

I have come to believe that the number of books a person reads is very nearly the least interesting fact about their reading, and that the practice which actually changes how a mind works is rereading, which almost nobody talks about and which is difficult to defend in a culture that measures literacy in volume. A first reading is an act of orientation. You are learning where the rooms are, and you are necessarily too busy following the plot or the argument to notice how the thing is built. Everything that is interesting about a book becomes visible only on the second pass, when you already know where it ends and can therefore attend to how it gets there.

The clearest case is the mystery, where the mechanics are unavoidable. On a first reading of a good detective novel you are engaged in a contest with the author, and your attention is entirely instrumental: you are looking for the clue, filtering everything else as noise. On a second reading, knowing the answer, you can finally see the extraordinary craft involved in placing that clue where it was both fully visible and completely unremarkable, and you notice that three quarters of the book is doing work you were too preoccupied to register. The book was never really about who did it. It was about the arrangement of your attention, and you cannot see an arrangement while you are inside it.

The same thing is true of arguments, and here it matters more. When I read a difficult essay for the first time I am mostly deciding whether I agree, and that decision consumes enough of my attention that I retain almost nothing about the structure of the reasoning. I come away with a verdict and a few quotable sentences. If I return to it a year later the verdict is already settled, and the reading becomes something else entirely: I can watch where the author chose to concede, where a difficult step is smuggled past in a subordinate clause, where a paragraph is doing rhetorical rather than logical work. It is only then that I learn anything about how to argue, which is presumably why the essays that shaped my thinking are without exception ones I have read at least three times.

There is an obvious objection, which is that time spent rereading is time not spent encountering something new, and that a person who rereads is trading breadth for depth in a world where breadth is what pays. I think this objection is correct about the trade and wrong about its terms. The relevant comparison is not between a reread book and a new book but between a reread book and the honest fate of most first readings, which is to be forgotten almost completely within a year. If I read twenty books and remember something real from three of them, I have not acquired twenty books' worth of anything. Rereading is not a sacrifice of breadth. It is a correction to a wildly optimistic accounting of what a single reading actually leaves behind.

What I have noticed practically is that rereading is unpleasant for about the first twenty pages and then becomes better than new reading. The unpleasantness is a specific feeling of waste, a low-grade anxiety that says you already know this and there are so many books you do not. It passes, and what replaces it is a kind of ease I have not found anywhere else, because you are no longer spending anything on comprehension and the entire budget is available for noticing. Almost every insight I have had about how prose works arrived in that state.

I keep a short list, six or seven titles, that I return to on a rough rotation without any expectation of finishing. The list has changed twice in fifteen years. Two of the books are novels I did not much like the first time and now consider indispensable, which is its own argument: a first reading is not even a reliable guide to whether you like something, because what you are evaluating on a first reading is largely the experience of not yet understanding it.

None of this is a prescription. Reading widely is a genuine good and I do not want to be the person who makes an ordinary pleasure into a discipline. But if you have ever finished a book with the uneasy sense that you had consumed rather than read it, the remedy is not a better book. It is the same book, in a year, when you have stopped needing to find out what happens.

Weiße Bohnensuppe mit Rosmarin und Zitronenschale

Veröffentlicht am 3. November 2022 von Katrin · 14 Kommentare · Kategorie: Suppen

Diese Suppe ist das Gegenteil von aufwendig, und trotzdem schmeckt sie nach mehr Arbeit, als sie macht. Das Geheimnis liegt nicht in einer besonderen Zutat, sondern darin, dass ein Teil der Bohnen püriert und der Rest ganz gelassen wird. Dadurch entsteht eine cremige Grundlage, ohne dass Sahne oder Mehl nötig sind, und die ganzen Bohnen geben der Suppe genug Struktur, damit sie als Hauptgericht durchgeht.

Wichtig ist der Rosmarin. Er wird nicht mitgekocht, sondern in heißem Öl kurz ausgezogen und zum Schluss darübergegeben. Mitgekocht wird Rosmarin nach zwanzig Minuten bitter und schmeckt vage nach Kiefer; kurz in Öl gebraten wird er nüssig und bleibt aromatisch. Das ist der einzige Schritt, bei dem man etwas falsch machen kann, und er dauert vierzig Sekunden.

Zutaten

Für vier Portionen als Hauptgericht oder sechs als Vorspeise:

  • 500 g getrocknete weiße Bohnen, über Nacht eingeweicht, oder drei Dosen Cannellini
  • 1 große Zwiebel, fein gewürfelt
  • 2 Stangen Sellerie, fein gewürfelt
  • 4 Knoblauchzehen, zwei gehackt und zwei ganz
  • 1 Parmesanrinde, falls vorhanden
  • 1,5 l Gemüsebrühe oder Bohnenkochwasser
  • 2 Zweige Rosmarin
  • Schale einer unbehandelten Zitrone
  • Gutes Olivenöl, Salz, schwarzer Pfeffer

Zubereitung

Die eingeweichten Bohnen abgießen, mit frischem Wasser und den zwei ganzen Knoblauchzehen aufsetzen und ohne Salz weich kochen, was je nach Alter der Bohnen zwischen fünfundvierzig Minuten und zwei Stunden dauert. Salz erst am Ende zugeben, sonst bleiben die Schalen zäh. Das Kochwasser nicht weggießen, es ist die beste Brühe für diese Suppe.

Zwiebel und Sellerie in reichlich Olivenöl bei mittlerer Hitze etwa zwölf Minuten anschwitzen, bis sie vollkommen weich und noch farblos sind. Das ist die zweite Stelle, an der Geduld sich bezahlt: angebräuntes Gemüse gibt der Suppe eine süßliche Note, die hier nicht hingehört. Den gehackten Knoblauch eine Minute mitbraten.

Zwei Drittel der Bohnen zugeben, mit Brühe auffüllen, die Parmesanrinde hineinlegen und zwanzig Minuten leise sieden lassen. Die Rinde entfernen, die Hälfte der Suppe mit dem Stabmixer pürieren, das letzte Drittel der ganzen Bohnen unterrühren und alles noch fünf Minuten ziehen lassen. Kräftig salzen, mehr als man denkt.

Zum Schluss vier Esslöffel Olivenöl in einer kleinen Pfanne heiß werden lassen, die Rosmarinnadeln hineingeben, vierzig Sekunden braten, bis sie knistern und dunkelgrün sind, und sofort vom Feuer nehmen. Die Suppe in Teller füllen, das Rosmarinöl darüber verteilen, Zitronenschale darüber reiben und mit grob gemahlenem Pfeffer servieren.

Anmerkungen

Die Suppe wird am zweiten Tag besser und am dritten am besten, wird dabei aber deutlich dicker. Mit heißem Wasser verdünnen, nicht mit kalter Brühe, und das Rosmarinöl jedes Mal frisch machen, es hält sich nicht.

Ohne Parmesanrinde fehlt etwas Tiefe. Ein Teelöffel Miso oder eine kleine Menge Sojasauce ersetzt sie erstaunlich gut und macht das Rezept vegan.

14 Kommentare

Beate am 4. November 2022:

Habe die Suppe gestern gemacht und war skeptisch wegen der Zitronenschale, aber sie ist wirklich der Punkt, an dem das Gericht aufwacht. Ohne sie ist es eine gute Bohnensuppe, mit ihr etwas anderes. Danke für das Rezept.

Jonas am 5. November 2022:

Wie lange halten sich die Bohnen im Kühlschrank, wenn ich sie vorkoche?

Katrin am 5. November 2022:

Im Kochwasser und gut abgedeckt vier bis fünf Tage, eingefroren drei Monate. Immer im Wasser einfrieren, sonst werden sie mehlig.

Chair's Statement

Extracted from the Annual Report and Financial Statements for the year ended 31 March 2023.

This has been a year in which the Trust did fewer things and did them for longer, and I want to use this statement to explain that choice rather than to celebrate it, because it involved disappointing a number of organisations we care about.

When I became Chair three years ago the Trust made ninety four grants a year with a median size of eleven thousand pounds and a median duration of twelve months. We were, on paper, a busy and responsive funder. In practice we were asking small organisations to spend a significant share of a small grant on the administration of applying for and reporting on it, and then to do the same thing again eleven months later. Our own staff spent roughly forty percent of their time on assessment and monitoring, which is to say on activity that produced no charitable outcome whatsoever.

In the year under review we made thirty one grants with a median size of sixty thousand pounds and a median duration of three years, and we made almost all of them unrestricted. Total charitable expenditure rose by four percent. The number of organisations we support fell by two thirds.

What we learned

The first thing we learned is that unrestricted multi-year funding is not simply a nicer version of restricted project funding. It changes what grantees do. Six of our thirty one partners used the certainty to hire their first permanent finance or fundraising staff, roles which are almost impossible to fund from project grants and which measurably improve an organisation's ability to survive. Two used it to end programmes that were not working, which no project grant has ever enabled anybody to do.

The second thing we learned is that our assessment process had been measuring the wrong thing with impressive rigour. Our old scoring framework rewarded organisations that were good at writing applications, and after reviewing four years of outcomes we could find no relationship at all between an applicant's assessment score and what subsequently happened with the money. We have replaced the framework with a conversation, a site visit, and a short internal note, and we will report in three years on whether this was wise.

The third thing, which is uncomfortable, is that concentration increases our influence over the organisations we fund whether we want it or not. When a grant represents a fifth of an organisation's income, our questions stop being questions. We have adopted a policy of not exceeding twenty five percent of any partner's turnover and of stating in writing at the outset that renewal is not contingent on following our advice, but we are aware that a policy does not remove a power imbalance, it only documents it.

Finances

The endowment stood at £148.2 million at the year end, down from £161.7 million, a fall of 8.3 percent driven almost entirely by the bond allocation. Total return over the trailing ten years remains 6.1 percent annualised against our long-term requirement of inflation plus four percent, which we continue to meet, though by a narrower margin than at any point since 2011.

Charitable expenditure was £6.4 million, representing 4.3 percent of the opening endowment value, slightly above our 4.0 percent policy rate. The Board has agreed to maintain expenditure in cash terms next year rather than reducing it in line with the endowment, accepting a modest real erosion of capital, on the grounds that our partners' costs are rising faster than our assets are falling.

Governance

Two trustees completed their second terms and stood down in September, and I record the Board's thanks to both. We recruited three new trustees through open advertisement rather than through the networks of existing trustees, for the first time in the Trust's history, and the resulting Board is the first in which a majority of members have direct experience of the circumstances our grants address.

The Board reviewed its own effectiveness with external facilitation in January. The review was blunt about the length of our meetings and about a tendency to revisit settled decisions, and we have reduced meetings from four hours to two and a half and adopted a written rule about reopening matters. I mention this partly because governance reviews are usually reported in language that conveys nothing.

Thanks

My thanks go to the staff team, who absorbed a change in strategy that made their existing expertise partly redundant, and who said so honestly and then got on with it. And to our partners, several of whom told us candidly that our old process was a burden, at some risk to themselves. We would not have changed without that.

Elizabeth Nkemdirim
Chair of Trustees
18 July 2023
